title: Linden Clinic: 100 more articles, or 3 better pages?
question: A fictional clinic wants more qualified enquiries. Should it scale the blog or improve its service pages first?
context: Illustrative scenario. No real client website or analytics was audited. Every demo-* observation is fictional. The first implementation phase is two weeks; revenue and conversion baselines are unknown.
assumptions: Demand for specific services is plausible but must be researched.
The owner can verify enquiry delivery and lead quality.

evidence.title: Twelve service pages, one recycled introduction
evidence.summary: Fictional sample: twelve service pages repeat the introduction, heading and generic call to action. This is scenario data, not a finding from a real website.

evidence.title: Button clicks counted as leads
evidence.summary: The demo analytics counts button clicks. Message delivery and enquiry quality are unverified; revenue is unknown.

evidence.title: Profile hours and services need verification
evidence.summary: The fictional clinic has not reconciled opening hours, services and contact paths between its business profile and website.

evidence.title: One AI answer does not mention the clinic
evidence.summary: One fictional answer is a research lead, not evidence that the brand is absent from all AI search.

evidence.title: Google: AI features and your website
evidence.summary: Check official requirements for participation in AI features separately from tool marketing and practitioner claims.
evidence.locator: Google Search Central / AI features documentation

evidence.title: Google: helpful, reliable, people-first content
evidence.summary: Primary guidance for assessing content usefulness and reliability. This source alone does not prove that a particular page is defective.
evidence.locator: Google Search Central / helpful content documentation

turns.text: Find the clinic through a patient's eyes. If its hours and services disagree across the web, a hundred new articles just send more people into the same confusion. Start with an accurate profile and a useful service page.
turns.challenge: I will change priorities if the profile is already accurate, visible for relevant searches and producing qualified enquiries.

turns.text: Twelve pages wearing the same introduction is one idea in twelve lab coats. Check crawl access and rendering, then add real detail about the treatment, practitioner and appointment. A shared template alone proves nothing.
turns.challenge: Show sampled source HTML, rendered content and meaningful page differences. A repeated template is not automatically a search-policy violation.

turns.text: Before article number one hundred about tooth decay, find the question asked by someone ready to book. One convincing service page may do more useful work than a library with no next step.
turns.challenge: I will support broader content when demand research shows how it helps a patient choose and book.

turns.text: A beautiful chart of button clicks is not revenue. We have not even checked whether the form arrives. Define a qualified enquiry and find where the patient journey breaks before buying more traffic.
turns.challenge: If enquiries already arrive and become appointments, we can discuss scaling acquisition.

turns.text: One AI answer without the brand is one answer, not a channel diagnosis. Record a repeatable set of patient questions, cited sources and conditions. Otherwise we are optimizing the mood of a single prompt.
turns.challenge: Evidence about actual patient journeys may show that AI is not an important channel for this clinic yet.

turns.text: The report needs to explain where patients came from, not just serve green arrows. Separate existing brand demand from new discovery and stop counting technical clicks as enquiries.
turns.challenge: Budget decisions need spend, valid conversions and enquiry quality. Those inputs are missing.

turns.text: 'Personalized care' is what everyone says. Who treats me, what happens at the appointment, and how do I book? Start with one page that helps a real person make that decision.
turns.challenge: If the page already answers those questions and converts relevant visitors, the problem may be further up the funnel.

turns.text: A fashionable new stack will not deliver a missing email by magic. Walk the form from a phone to the inbox and keep a working backup. Diagnosis costs less than a holy war about the CMS.
turns.challenge: I will support a migration when specific requirements cannot reasonably be implemented and maintained on the current site.

turns.text: Neil, measurement matters, but the wrong opening hours can lose a patient today. I want profile verification alongside form QA, not parked behind a tracking project. Kate's page work only helps after the patient reaches it.
turns.challenge: I will change priorities if the profile is already accurate, visible for relevant searches and producing qualified enquiries.

turns.text: Edward, intent is a sensible bet; a technical diagnosis still needs a test. I will not put 'fix indexation' on this plan until we inspect directives and rendering. Duplicate phrasing is a content observation, not an indexation verdict.
turns.challenge: Show sampled source HTML, rendered content and meaningful page differences. A repeated template is not automatically a search-policy violation.

turns.text: Neil, I accept the lead-quality gate. I still disagree with waiting for perfect attribution before researching demand. Let one high-intent query and a booking path define a small page experiment while measurement is being checked.
turns.challenge: I will support broader content when demand research shows how it helps a patient choose and book.

turns.text: TJ, an AI visibility dashboard is a distraction if the form drops enquiries. Keep the AI sample small and behind conversion QA. I would fund a verified path to an appointment before chasing a mention in one answer.
turns.challenge: If enquiries already arrive and become appointments, we can discuss scaling acquisition.

turns.text: Dan, agreed on testing the existing stack. Neil, I will keep AI work bounded, but a repeatable source sample is research, not a site rebuild. We can learn whether it deserves a budget without promising citations.
turns.challenge: Evidence about actual patient journeys may show that AI is not an important channel for this clinic yet.

turns.text: Neil, a working form is necessary, but a fired conversion can still be junk. Someone must reconcile test delivery with real patient intent. I want a written definition of a qualified enquiry before we celebrate an improved conversion rate.
turns.challenge: Budget decisions need spend, valid conversions and enquiry quality. Those inputs are missing.

turns.text: Harry, a short technical check earns its place. An endless checklist does not. Once the page works and is accessible, the next release should answer patient questions and make booking clear, not chase cosmetic audit points.
turns.challenge: If the page already answers those questions and converts relevant visitors, the problem may be further up the funnel.

turns.text: TJ, that scope works. My objection is to treating a platform change as the intervention. Keep the URL, make one reversible change in staging, and replay the same form test afterward so we can tell what changed.
turns.challenge: I will support a migration when specific requirements cannot reasonably be implemented and maintained on the current site.

turns.text: Test, with a condition: verify the profile in parallel with measurement. Local accuracy is part of the patient's route to the clinic, not a reward we unlock after the dashboard is perfect.
turns.challenge: I will change priorities if the profile is already accurate, visible for relevant searches and producing qualified enquiries.

turns.text: Test one service page after a short crawl-and-render check. I will own the technical acceptance list and keep every unverified indexation claim out of the final report.
turns.challenge: Show sampled source HTML, rendered content and meaningful page differences. A repeated template is not automatically a search-policy violation.

turns.text: Test one page against a researched booking-intent query. I still want demand research to start early; 'measure first' must not turn into 'learn nothing about the market for a month.'
turns.challenge: I will support broader content when demand research shows how it helps a patient choose and book.

turns.text: Test, then decide on scale. First validate enquiry delivery and quality. More content becomes a business choice once we can connect it to meaningful patient outcomes.
turns.challenge: If enquiries already arrive and become appointments, we can discuss scaling acquisition.

turns.text: Test the page; keep AI visibility exploratory. My deliverable is a repeatable observation log, not a promised mention, ranking or new platform.
turns.challenge: Evidence about actual patient journeys may show that AI is not an important channel for this clinic yet.

turns.text: Test with a written baseline and decision rule. We can accept the implementation in two weeks; we cannot guarantee that two weeks provides enough data for a commercial conclusion.
turns.challenge: Budget decisions need spend, valid conversions and enquiry quality. Those inputs are missing.

turns.text: Test a page that earns a booking: specific treatment information, a credible practitioner and an accessible next step. The clinic must verify every medical statement.
turns.challenge: If the page already answers those questions and converts relevant visitors, the problem may be further up the funnel.

turns.text: Test on the existing site with a backup and a reversible release. A passing mobile-to-inbox check is acceptance evidence. A new framework is not.
turns.challenge: I will support a migration when specific requirements cannot reasonably be implemented and maintained on the current site.

actions.title: Verify the path from form to qualified enquiry
actions.why: We cannot distinguish a real patient request from a technical click.
actions.acceptance: Test enquiries arrive, events do not duplicate, the qualified-enquiry definition is documented, and personal data stays out of the public report.

actions.title: Rework one priority service page
actions.why: Repeated generic text makes it hard to test whether the page helps a patient choose the clinic.
actions.acceptance: Medical facts, service details, practitioner information, booking conditions and accessible form are verified; the URL is preserved.

experiment.baseline: Record relevant visits, valid enquiries and available sample size before changing the page.
experiment.change: Change content and the booking path on one service page.
experiment.measure: Qualified enquiries and their share of relevant visits, with traffic sources recorded.
experiment.success: Agree the minimum useful business effect and sample requirements before launch; do not define success after seeing the result.
experiment.stop: Roll back for broken delivery, factual errors or degraded accessibility.
experiment.window: The first 14 days cover implementation QA. Make a business decision only after sufficient data, accounting for seasonality.

actions.title: Reconcile the profile, services and contact details
actions.why: Conflicting information can make it harder to trust or contact the business.
actions.acceptance: Details are confirmed with the owner and website; saved changes are checked and evidence is retained.

actions.title: Build a repeatable sample of AI answers
actions.why: One prompt cannot represent a channel. Establish an observable baseline first.
actions.acceptance: For each answer, record query, engine, date, context, mentions and links. Missing data is never reported as zero visibility.

verdict.summary: Start with reliable measurement and one useful service page. Defer blog expansion until demand, enquiry quality and content usefulness have been tested.
verdict.dissent: Edward wants booking-intent research to start earlier. Darren puts profile accuracy alongside measurement. Keep both conditions in the first phase rather than hiding them behind a unanimous vote.
verdict.unknowns: Real search demand, page accessibility, GSC/GA4 data, appointment conversion, service economics and the role of AI in patient choice are unknown.
